title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation failure used for fraud. Scammers produced a fabricated news article depicting a confrontation between two real, named public figures, a Reserve Bank governor and a finance presenter, to lend credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The AI tools involved generated convincing text, images, and video of real people saying and doing things that never occurred. The failure is not in a single deployed AI product but in the use of generative AI capabilities, including deepfakes, as components of a coordinated deception infrastructure built around fake articles, reviews, websites, and advertisements.

Detection would have required either platform-level checks before publication or distribution of the fabricated content, or audience awareness that named public figures can be convincingly impersonated at scale. Neither was present. ASIC's figures show the volume of such scams rising sharply, which indicates that takedowns are reactive rather than preventive. The content reached potential investors before regulators acted.

What is not established is who specifically created the fabricated article or the Boulder Sparhaven platform, and no finding of liability against any AI model provider or hosting platform has been reported.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has highlighted a growing type of scam. The fabricated article described an increasingly heated interview between the two, with Bullock supposedly objecting to questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The confrontation never actually occurred. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows that AI-generated investment scams using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians are becoming more common and convincing. Last year, regulators took down 19,400 scams, up 182 percent, with phishing scams rising 279 percent and fake investment platforms increasing 151 percent.

Scammers now build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, websites, and advertisements to lure victims. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by other politicians and financial experts including Kohler, who has previously experienced similar scams. ASIC chair Sarah Court advises potential investors to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through the regulator's public registers and avoid investing if companies cannot provide legitimate credentials. Alan Kohler argues that penalties should extend to platforms hosting this content and companies creating the AI models used in scams.
